strengths: The paper identifies an important and timely problem: continual adaptation of LLM-based generative recommenders, where preserving old behavior is not always the right objective because preferences drift.

The proposed PESO method is simple, efficient, and easy to implement: a single evolving LoRA adapter plus a proximal regularizer to the previous adapter. Its storage advantage over cumulative adapter methods is clear.

The empirical section is broader than many submissions in this area, with multiple Amazon domains, an additional Yelp result, several cumulative LoRA variants, traditional continual recommender comparisons, alternative regularizers, another backbone, learning-rate analysis, and efficiency discussion.
The analysis in Section 3 usefully shows that cumulative LoRA variants can behave differently under user-disjoint versus natural chronological splits, which helps motivate the design choice.
The presentation is generally clear, and the paper provides enough implementation detail to understand the method and reproduce the main setup in principle.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited. PESO is essentially proximal regularization of LoRA parameters toward the previous checkpoint, with a softmax-KL variant. This is conceptually close to standard continual-learning regularization and parameter anchoring, and the paper does not fully establish why this particular softmax-KL form is fundamentally new or preferable.

The theoretical contribution is mostly interpretive and relies on strong approximations: linearization of logits, an MSE surrogate for cross-entropy, a quadratic approximation around an inaccessible optimum, and fixed tangent features. The resulting direction-wise interpolation is a standard property of quadratic objectives with proximal terms, so it provides limited evidence about the actual nonlinear LLM recommender training dynamics.

The softmax-KL regularizer over raw LoRA parameters is not fully justified. Softmax discards absolute scale and sign structure, has shift-invariant null directions within each group, and may regularize parameter distributions rather than functionally meaningful behavior. The paper gives empirical comparisons but little principled argument for why this geometry is appropriate for LoRA matrices.

The empirical gains, while consistent, are often small in absolute terms, especially on Books and Movies & TV. The paper does not report variance across seeds or statistical significance, making it hard to judge whether the improvements are robust enough for a top-tier claim.

There are evaluation/protocol ambiguities. The text says models are updated through D5 but main results are averaged over D2 through D4, and it is unclear why D5 is excluded. It is also unclear whether the semantic-ID tokenizer/codebook is trained only on past data or on all items, which could introduce future-item information leakage in a continual setting.

The evaluation is mostly on processed Amazon-style implicit feedback with constrained generation. The paper would be stronger with clearer discussion of candidate-space assumptions, cold-start/new-item handling, and whether constrained beam search plus fixed semantic IDs reflects deployable continual recommendation.

Some baseline comparisons may not be fully balanced. PESO receives a tuned regularization coefficient, but it is not always clear whether all baselines received equally careful tuning under the same continual protocol, especially for cumulative LoRA and traditional recommender methods.

The forgetting analysis is somewhat underdeveloped: PESO sometimes forgets more than cumulative LoRA on past blocks, and the claim that this is benign/adaptive is plausible but not rigorously validated beyond selected dormant/new user group metrics.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and timely problem: continual adaptation of LLM-based generative recommenders under temporal preference drift.
The proposed method is simple and practical: adding a proximal regularizer to a single evolving LoRA adapter has low storage and computational overhead compared with cumulative-adapter approaches.

The paper includes several useful empirical comparisons, including multiple Amazon categories, several cumulative LoRA variants, additional PEFT baselines in the appendix, and a small analysis of dormant vs. new users.
The exposition is generally understandable, and the authors make a reasonable conceptual point that preserving past-task accuracy is not always the right objective for recommendation.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is limited. PESO is essentially proximal regularization of LoRA parameters, and the theory reduces to a standard quadratic/ridge-style interpolation result under strong linearization and MSE surrogate assumptions. This does not substantially justify the specific method beyond known stability-plasticity intuitions.

The main empirical gains are small in absolute terms and often marginal: e.g., improvements over single evolving LoRA are around 0.0002 to 0.0011 NDCG/Hit in several settings, with Books H@5 tied. No variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported, making it unclear whether the claimed improvements are robust.

The parameter-space softmax-KL regularizer is not well justified for LoRA. LoRA factors are non-identifiable under rescaling of A and B while preserving BA, so regularizing raw flattened A/B coordinates can depend on arbitrary factor scaling rather than model function. The paper does not address this issue.

The evaluation protocol raises concerns. The text inconsistently describes stages D2-D5 but reports averages over D2-D4, leaving ambiguity about whether the final block is used for testing, tuning, or omitted. Hyperparameter selection details are also too sparse to assess fairness across baselines.

The strongest claims about stability and plasticity are only weakly supported. Dormant/new user analysis is limited to one dataset and one metric, while the explicit forgetting table shows PESO can forget more than baselines on several past blocks, which complicates the narrative.

Baseline treatment is not fully convincing. Some cumulative LoRA variants perform extremely poorly, suggesting possible implementation or tuning issues, and the paper does not provide enough detail to rule this out. Traditional recommender comparisons are also compressed and appear to use unclear averaged metrics.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a top-tier submission: the abstract contains an unfinished code availability sentence, and the reproducibility statement only promises release upon publication. Important implementation details such as seeds, hardware, training epochs, batch sizes, LoRA ranks/target modules, and decoding settings are incomplete or scattered.

The paper overclaims relative to evidence, repeatedly stating consistent superiority and broad applicability despite modest gains, limited domains, no significance testing, and a method whose main advantage may be ordinary regularization plus tuned learning rates.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: continual adaptation of LLM-based generative recommender systems under evolving users, items, and preferences.

The motivation is well articulated. The distinction between stability/plasticity in recommendation versus standard class-incremental vision settings is convincing and helps justify why cumulative LoRA may be inappropriate.
PESO is simple, efficient, and well matched to the problem: maintaining a single evolving adapter with a proximal regularizer avoids the storage growth and rigidity of accumulating adapters.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this problem, covering multiple Amazon categories, an additional Yelp dataset, multiple continual LoRA baselines, traditional continual recommender baselines, and an alternate backbone.

Results are consistent: PESO is usually best or tied for best across metrics, with particularly clear improvements over cumulative LoRA variants and other continual PEFT baselines on the main datasets.
The paper includes useful ablations on regularizer choice, proximal weight, learning rate, user groups, distribution shift, and forgetting, which strengthen the empirical story.
The theoretical analysis provides helpful intuition for why proximal regularization can yield direction-wise interpolation between preserving the previous adapter and adapting to new data.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate. Proximal regularization toward the previous parameters is a well-established idea in continual learning; the main contribution is its application and tailoring to LoRA-based generative recommendation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical analysis relies on strong simplifications: linearized logits, an MSE surrogate for cross-entropy, local quadratic approximations, and fixed LoRA subspace assumptions. It is useful for intuition but does not strongly explain behavior in the actual autoregressive LLM training regime.

The empirical gains, while consistent, are often small in absolute terms and sometimes modest in relative terms, especially on Books and Movies & TV. The paper does not report variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance, making it hard to assess robustness.

There is some ambiguity/inconsistency in the temporal evaluation description: the paper defines D2 through D5 but reports averages over D2 through D4 in places. This should be clarified because excluding the final block could affect the continual-learning conclusions.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The abstract appears to leave the code URL blank, and the reproducibility statement says code will be released upon publication. Important details such as random seeds, compute budget, exact preprocessing artifacts, and tokenizer training details could be more explicit.

The comparison to full retraining is somewhat limited. The paper argues that sequential LoRA can outperform cumulative retraining, but cumulative retraining settings, recency weighting, replay, or stronger retraining schedules are not explored in depth.

The forgetting analysis is not entirely favorable to PESO: PESO has larger drops on some past blocks than alternatives, and the claim that this is benign/adaptive is plausible but not fully substantiated beyond aggregate performance and a small user-group analysis.

Ethical and societal discussion is brief. Since recommender systems can amplify exposure bias and preference lock-in, a stronger discussion of how continual adaptation may affect bias, popularity amplification, or user manipulation would improve the paper.
